---
name: flow-steward-contribute-code
description: Use when a contributor wants to fix a bug or propose an improvement in the Flow Steward core repository Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app; covers the issue, fork and branch, the Development environment, the regression test, the lint.sh quality tiers, commits, the pull request with evidence and the review loop.
---

# Contribute Code to Flow Steward

The core repository is <https://github.com/Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app>
(Apache-2.0). Issues and pull requests go there. Extensions and workflow
templates are published elsewhere: use `flow-steward-publish-extension` for an
extension; a workflow template goes to <https://github.com/Flow-Steward/workflows>,
whose README explains the submission.

The repository's own rules win over this skill. Read, in this order:
`AGENTS.md`, `docs/standards/README.md`, `docs/standards/agent-workflow-standard.md`,
`docs/standards/testing-standard.md`, then the standard for the area you touch
(`architecture-standard.md`, `backend-python-standard.md`,
`frontend-standard.md`, `security-standard.md`, `configuration-standard.md`).
Security vulnerabilities go privately to `security@flow-steward.org`
(`SECURITY.md`), never to a public issue or pull request.

This work needs a terminal with Git and Docker, a full clone of the
repository, and GitHub access (your client's GitHub tools or an authenticated
`gh`) for the fork and the pull request. It does not need a Flow Steward MCP
connection. When one of them is missing, say which and what it blocks: without
a terminal or clone no change can be made or verified; without GitHub the user
pushes and opens the pull request from your prepared branch and description.

## 1. Start from an issue

Search the issues first (`gh issue list --repo Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app --state all --search "<words>"`).
If none exists, open one (the `flow-steward-report-issue` skill) and describe
the problem and the change you propose. For anything larger than a small bug
fix — a new feature, a changed contract, a database change, a new dependency,
a new architectural pattern — wait for a maintainer to agree on the approach
before starting the change. One issue, one pull request, one change.

## 2. Fork, clone and branch

```bash
gh repo fork Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app --clone
cd flow-steward-app
git switch -c fix/<issue-number>-<short-slug>
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit
```

Use a full clone, not a shallow one. Keep the branch on top of the latest
`main` (`git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main`).

## 3. Development environment

Work in the **Development** environment, never on a production installation:

```bash
./install.sh --environment development --file-storage bundled
./flow-steward status
./flow-steward doctor
```

It runs the core plus the frontend and keeps the `fs-test-runner` and
`fs-audit` containers ready for tests and quality gates. Docker with Compose v2
runs the product and every test; never treat a test run with a host Python or
Node as evidence.
`./flow-steward environment show` tells which environment is installed. Set
`FS_AUTO_RELOAD=1` for backend reload, and start `fs-frontend` for Vite hot
reload (see the repository's `docs/GUIDE.md`).

## 4. Make the change

- Find the owning code and its tests first; read callers before changing a
  function.
- Put code where `AGENTS.md` says: `core/entrypoints/` only adapts transports,
  `core/application/` holds business logic, `core/infrastructure/` holds
  technical adapters. Frontend code lives in `assets/frontend/` and reuses the
  existing components.
- **Bug fix: write the regression test first** and watch it fail for the
  expected reason before fixing.
- Database changes after 1.0 are SQL files in
  `db/migrations/YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_slug.sql`; `db/schema/` is the 1.0 baseline.
- Update docs in the same pull request when behavior, a command, an API or a
  setting changes. An architectural decision needs an ADR in
  `docs/architecture/adr/`.
- Keep unrelated cleanup out of the change.

After each edit batch, format only the files you changed:

```bash
python -m ruff check --fix <changed-python-files>
python -m ruff format <changed-python-files>
cd assets/frontend && npx --no-install eslint --fix <changed-ts-or-tsx-files>
```

## 5. Verify in tiers

Every tier runs in the disposable `fs-audit` container through
`./core/entrypoints/cli/scripts/lint.sh`.

| Tier | When | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | during the fix, fail-fast | `./core/entrypoints/cli/scripts/lint.sh --checks targeted-tests --test-paths "auto tests/unit/<regression_test>.py"` and, for frontend changes, `--checks frontend-targeted-tests --test-paths auto` |
| 2 | before each commit (the pre-commit hook runs it) | `./core/entrypoints/cli/scripts/lint.sh --fast` |
| 3 | once, from the final commit, before the pull request | `./core/entrypoints/cli/scripts/lint.sh --full` |

`auto` selects tests from your diff against `main`; add by path what the import
graph cannot see (runtime, database, extension tests). Diagnose a failure
before rerunning it. `--full` runs the whole backend suite without stopping at
the first failure: group the failures by root cause and fix them as one batch.
Never commit with `--no-verify`. GitHub Actions are disabled in this
repository, so your local gate result is the evidence reviewers see.

## 6. Commit

Commit when Tier 2 passes. Write a plain one-line summary of what changes for
the user or the code, for example
`Keep every lane's writes when parallel lanes finish together`, and a body
that says why. Reference the issue (`Refs #123`). Do not commit secrets,
`.env` files, logs, screenshots, task plans or audit reports.

## 7. Pull request

```bash
git push -u origin fix/<issue-number>-<short-slug>
gh pr create --repo Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app --base main --title "<summary>" --body-file pr.md
```

The description contains:

- `Fixes #<issue>` (or `Refs #<issue>` for partial work);
- what was wrong and what changed, in a few sentences;
- how it was verified: the exact commands, their exit codes, and the commit
  SHA `--full` ran on; the regression test name; for UI changes, before and
  after screenshots without private data;
- risk and anything not verified (for example: not tried on ARM64, not tried
  on Scalable).

## 8. Review loop

Answer every review comment, either with a change or with a reason. Push
fixes as new commits on the same branch; rerun Tier 1 for the touched area and
`--fast` before each commit, and `--full` again on the final commit before you
ask for another review. Update the description's evidence with the new SHA.
Do not merge your own pull request; a maintainer merges it.
flow-steward-developer.skills/flow-steward-extension-authoring/:
---
name: flow-steward-extension-authoring
description: Use when a developer or integrator wants to create or change a Flow Steward extension bundle using the platform's existing manifest and CLI lifecycle.
---

# Flow Steward Extension Authoring

Build against the target release's contracts and existing lifecycle. Keep
provider logic in the extension's out-of-process runtime.

This work needs a terminal with Docker, a Flow Steward application checkout of
the target release installed in the Development environment, and the
extension's own checkout. It does not need a Flow Steward MCP connection or
token. When the terminal or the checkout is missing, say which one and stop
before writing files you cannot validate; never report an unvalidated bundle
as ready.

## Locate the contracts

Find the target Flow Steward application checkout. Read `AGENTS.md`, applicable
`docs/standards/*`, `docs/standards/extension-manifest-standard.yaml`, and
`docs/extension-authoring-agent-playbook.md`. Locate its version-matched
documentation checkout for `docs/integrations/build-an-extension.md`,
`docs/developer/extensions.md` and `docs/reference/cli.md`; the playbook identifies
fallbacks when supporting docs are unavailable. Report gaps instead of inventing
flags. Do not assume an absolute machine path or repository-relative links from
this copied skill folder.

Choose a compatible reference exercising the required features; Core bundles no
reference extension. <https://github.com/Flow-Steward/ext-example-showcase>
implements every extension feature and is the default reference. Inspect its manifest, contracts and representative runtime
handlers. Keep schemas in their canonical owners rather than copying them here.

## Choose the authored contracts

`extensions create` writes a minimal `tool_provider` at version `1.0.0`, with
features `[tool, action]`, empty `event_subscriptions`, and a sample
`save_settings` action with `workflow_visible: false`. It does not generate a
workflow-visible tool action or a finished task/notification provider. Choose
`tool_provider` + `tool`, `task_provider` + `task_ingress`, or
`notification_provider` + `notify`, then replace the sample contracts and
handlers together; changing kind/features alone is insufficient.

For workflow use, explicitly set the action's `workflow_visible: true` and
supply a same-ID visible Contract V2 operation. Visible operations need the
same-ID visible action in the other direction too. Active workflow-visible
actions require Contract V2; merely exposing the settings action in UI does
not make it callable from a workflow. Keep configuration/delivery actions
hidden where their contracts require `workflow_visible: false`.

Flow Steward deliberately has no inline code step. When a user asks for "a
code step", build an action with `workflow_visible: true` plus a same-ID
Contract V2 operation, and call it from the workflow's Extension tools step.

### Host contract and logo

`runtime.contract_version` must be `extension_host_v2`, the one host contract
Flow Steward 1.0 runs; the scaffold writes it. Build runtime code on the public
`flowsteward-extension-sdk` (0.4.0 or later), never on private Core modules.
The bundle's logo is a file named `icon.png` next to `extension.yaml`: a square
PNG of 32–512 px (128×128 recommended), at most 100 KB. There is no manifest
field for it. The scaffold writes a neutral default icon; replace it before
publishing. The archive installer validates the icon.

Declare the extension's outbound network access under `egress` (an extension
that makes no outbound calls declares `egress: {}`); without it, installation
warns `egress_undeclared`.

### Task ingress

Declare these reserved action/query contracts and implement their runtime
responses. Every listed `result_fields` value and `error_codes` entry is required:

| Operation | Kind | Result fields | Required errors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `normalize_task_action` | Action | `result.normalized` | `not_configured`, `authentication_failed`, `invalid_payload`, `rate_limited`, `provider_unavailable`, `timeout`, `internal_error` |
| `fetch_attachments` | Action | `result.attachments` | `not_configured`, `authentication_failed`, `not_found`, `rate_limited`, `provider_unavailable`, `timeout`, `internal_error` |
| `sync_completion_status` | Action | `result.status` | `not_configured`, `authentication_failed`, `conflict`, `rate_limited`, `provider_unavailable`, `timeout`, `internal_error` |
| `provider_health` | Query | `result.status`, `result.configured` | `not_configured`, `authentication_failed`, `provider_unavailable`, `timeout`, `internal_error` |

All declared action/query errors for this profile must come from the target
release's `TASK_INGRESS_ERROR_CODES` catalog in
`core/infrastructure/db/ingress_runtime.py`; additional invented errors fail
validation. The generated health query's smaller error set is insufficient for
this profile. Do not invent a polling/ack operation to replace the reserved IDs.

### Notification delivery and ingress events

An active notification provider reserves exactly one `deliver_notification`
action, same-ID V2 operation and external effect:

- Action: `handler.mode: extension`, `workflow_visible: false`, exactly required
  object parameters `event` and `route`.
- V2 operation: `operation_kind: action`, `workflow_visible: false`, exactly
  required object inputs `event` and `route`; outputs include `delivered`
  (`boolean`) and `provider_message_id` (`text`).
- Effect: `operation_id: deliver_notification`, `effect_kind: message_delivery`,
  nonempty `channel`, `idempotency: required`, `test_mode_behavior: suppress`.

`release_stage: placeholder` exempts delivery validation, but does not exempt
kind/features and cannot be enabled. It is not a working notification provider.

Author `event_subscriptions`; compilation derives `supported_events`. Writing
`supported_events` directly in the manifest fails with `unknown_manifest_field`.
The `ingress_event` feature is notification-provider-only and requires an
`ingress_event` action with `result_fields: [result.ingress_type]` and selector:

```yaml
event_subscriptions:
  - event_type: external.comment.received
    severity: any
    conditions: {}
```

`notification.interaction_received` is recommended, not required. Subscriptions
and ingress handling do not replace the reserved delivery contract.

Phase events no longer exist. Subscribe to the current job events, such as
`job.group_*`, `job.approval_waiting` and `job.timer_waiting`.

### Own namespace grants and distribution metadata

Declare only needed `runtime_grants.resources` / `runtime_grants.mutations`
from the manifest standard. Host grants cover the owning extension's data:
`scope` may only be `owning_extension`, and a `provider_key` may only equal the
extension's own ID; relevant kinds default to those values. Foreign namespaces,
unknown kinds or malformed `secret_keys` / `connection_type_ids` lists fail
with `runtime_grant_forbidden`. Vendor identity or catalog verification grants
no extra rights; use the public SDK rather than private Core imports.

Runtime manifest vendor metadata uses `vendor.name`; the strict
`extension-descriptor.yaml` vendor model requires `vendor.vendor_name` and
rejects unknown fields. The descriptor uses
`schema_version: extension_descriptor_v1` and `release_version`, not manifest
`version`. Its release version defaults to `1.0.0`, so set it explicitly when
changing the manifest version. Archive manifest `extension_id` and `version`
must match descriptor `extension_id` and `release_version`. Descriptor
`platform_version` in a validation request selects host compatibility, not the
extension release. Marketplace manifest checks do not validate this descriptor
shape. Validate both surfaces before packaging/importing.

## Author and verify

Work from an installed, healthy Development source environment. Use the public
Docker-backed `./flow-steward` launcher and current `extensions --help` plus
subcommand help. The public module is `python -m core.entrypoints.cli` inside
the supported runtime; private CLI modules are not executable alternatives.
Do not use host pytest or a host virtual environment for platform verification.

1. Define the extension ID, behavior and operation input/output contracts.
   Scaffold through `extensions create` or adapt the chosen compatible reference.
   Implement only the requested features, using the canonical YAML manifest,
   bundle-local references and public extension SDK/runtime contracts.
2. Run `extensions validate` and focused `extensions test`. Repair actual
   contract/runtime failures before packaging. Health checks can execute the
   extension's health command; choose fixtures appropriate to the requested task.
   Testing requires `requirements-dev.txt`; dependencies install offline with
   `pip --no-index`, searching `dev-wheels/` and `wheels/`. Inherited tooling
   packages can satisfy requirements; supply compatible local wheels for missing
   development dependencies. Without `tests/test_*.py`, the run fails unless
   intentionally allowed with `--allow-no-pytest`; report the omitted coverage.
   Validation, smoke and dependency failures still fail the run.
3. For third-party Python dependencies, follow the target release's wheel guide
   and playbook: `extensions lock-deps` must lock the full transitive closure and
   wheel hashes, then `extensions bundle --with-wheels` must include portable
   wheels for both Linux AMD64 and ARM64. The default platforms are
   `manylinux2014_x86_64,manylinux2014_aarch64`, for the tooling interpreter's
   Python version/implementation/ABI, not every Python version. A compatible
   universal wheel may cover both; compiled dependencies require matching wheels
   and hashes for each. Use `--platforms active` only for an explicitly requested
   local-only bundle. If either target lacks compatible wheels, stop portable
   packaging and report the gap; do not silently omit a target or rely on runtime
   downloads.
   - The runtime is CPython 3.12 on glibc 2.36 (`python:3.12-slim`, Debian
     bookworm). For packages that publish only `manylinux_2_28` wheels, pass
     `--platforms manylinux_2_28_x86_64,manylinux_2_28_aarch64` to both
     `lock-deps` and `bundle`.
   - Plain fallback without the CLI: `pip download --only-binary=:all:
     --platform manylinux2014_x86_64` (and again with `manylinux2014_aarch64`)
     `--implementation cp --python-version 3.12 --abi cp312 --abi abi3 --abi none`,
     with each wheel's hash listed in `python_requirements`.
   - `extensions validate` does **not** check both architectures. Before
     handoff, list `wheels/` and confirm, for every requirement, an `_x86_64`
     and an `_aarch64` wheel, or one `any` wheel.
   - Archives are limited to 50 MiB zipped and 150 MiB unpacked. A pure-Python
     bundle over the limit can be split with `--runtime-target linux-amd64` and
     `--runtime-target linux-arm64`, one archive per architecture.

Native executables require two separately built and targeted archives using
`--runtime-target linux-amd64` and `--runtime-target linux-arm64`. Wheel tooling
is not a cross-compiler. Packaging and wheel coverage are not actual installation
verification on both architectures; report the environments and checks actually
run, including missing architecture coverage. Keep the full procedure in the
located `docs/integrations/build-an-extension.md` wheel/distribution guide.

The bare bundle example below is for zero third-party Python dependencies, from
the application checkout with a task-authorized new ID:

```bash
./flow-steward extensions create com.acme.example --non-interactive --confirm
./flow-steward extensions validate com.acme.example --root extensions --health
./flow-steward extensions test com.acme.example --root extensions --non-interactive
./flow-steward extensions bundle com.acme.example --root extensions --output-dir dist/extensions --non-interactive --confirm
```

The default scaffold version is `1.0.0`, so this example writes
`dist/extensions/com.acme.example-1.0.0.zip`. Use the reported archive path when
the manifest version changes. Bundle success reports packaging; retain the
separate validate/test results as evidence of those checks.

An extension kept in its own repository (outside the application checkout) is
checked by the application's quality gate, from the application checkout, with
an absolute path to the extension checkout:

```bash
./core/entrypoints/cli/scripts/lint.sh --checks extension-static,extension-tests --extension-root /abs/path/to/extension-checkout
```

`extension-static` runs compile, ruff, ruff format, mypy and bandit over the
bundle's modules; `extension-tests` is the `extensions test` path (validation,
then pytest in an offline venv). The checkout is copied into the gate
container, so commit first and cite that commit. To publish to the public
extension catalog, use the `flow-steward-publish-extension` skill.

`--root` is the parent containing the normalized bundle folder, not that folder.
The leaf `--confirm` accepts the reviewed create/package operation; it is not
permission for installation or publication. `extensions test` has no `--confirm`.
It requires the Development launcher's dedicated `fs-test-runner`; a generic
MCP or admin client can refuse. Report that limitation and use the supported
launcher, without setting `FS_EXTENSION_TEST_RUNTIME` to bypass it. Production
does not provision test tooling implicitly. Nonzero or review exits are not
successful validation.



## Observed CLI status example

A historical isolated Compact product-runtime check at source SHA
`968f373fd879fee10aa9136d5930761be81bab0c` observed the following.
These are process exit codes for that fixture, not compiler issue codes or a
fresh installed-launcher acceptance result:

| Fixture and command | Exit and observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Generated valid scaffold: `extensions create`, then `extensions validate` | Both `0`; create used `--non-interactive --confirm`. |
| Temporary manifest `kind: invalid_kind`: `extensions validate` | `3`, outer error `validation_failed`; unsupported manifest kind. |
| Same invalid manifest: `extensions bundle --non-interactive --confirm` | `0`; packaging wrote the versioned ZIP despite the invalid manifest. |
| Extract that ZIP, then `extensions validate` against the extracted root | `3`, `validation_failed`; the invalid manifest remains invalid. |
| `extensions test --non-interactive` outside the dedicated test runtime | `3`, `validation_failed`; runtime guard stopped before pytest/smoke. |

The bundle row is a negative demonstration, not permission to continue after
failed validation. In the normal validate/test/bundle sequence, stop on any
nonzero exit. This historical check does not establish scaffold pytest,
offline dependency behavior, authenticated descriptor API or installed catalog
acceptance. Run tests through the installed Development launcher and retain the
actual exit/status evidence for the target release.

## Descriptor API and validation diagnostics

Use an authenticated client with the target release's existing authority checks.
The registered endpoints are:

| POST route | Content type and request fields |
| --- | --- |
| `/api/extensions/descriptors/validate` | `application/json`: `source_type` (`file` by default, or `url`, `builtin`, `payload`), `descriptor_path`, `descriptor_url`, `descriptor_payload` (object), `source_root`, `platform_version` (default `1.0.0`), `allow_insecure_remote` (default `false`). For inline validation use `source_type: "payload"` and the descriptor object in `descriptor_payload`. |
| `/api/extensions/descriptors/import/file` | `application/json`: required `descriptor_path`, optional `install_after_import` (default `false`), `runtime_mode`, `remote_base_url`. The path must be accessible to the server. |
| `/api/extensions/descriptors/import/url` | `application/json`: required `descriptor_url`, optional `install_after_import` (default `false`), `runtime_mode`, `remote_base_url`. The server fetches the URL. |
| `/api/extensions/install` | `multipart/form-data`: required `file` containing the ZIP; optional `approved_browser_authority_impact_hash` (empty by default, or 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters) binds the reviewed browser-authority impact. |

A descriptor file import is not a client-side file upload. JSON request wrappers
are compatible with YAML-only bundle contracts. Keep import and installation
within the authorized task; `install_after_import` explicitly requests installation.

`extensions validate --marketplace` adds manifest checks for identity/display
fields, `vendor.name` (or `vendor_name`), listing category/summary, nonempty
required scopes, machine-auth service-account key/scopes, and account-scope
metadata. These checks do not replace descriptor validation. Archive validation
separately checks that manifest identity/version match descriptor
`extension_id`/`release_version`; inspect the imported release and catalog after
installation to verify the resulting identity and metadata.

Preserve each emitted issue's code, field/path and message when reporting failures:

| Emitted issue code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `extension.yaml_only_violation` | Forbidden JSON contract files; convert the contract and references to YAML. Runtime Python and JSON API wrappers are not prohibited by this issue. |
| `workflow_action_requires_contract_v2` | Workflow-visible actions require Contract V2. |
| `workflow_action_operation_mismatch` | A workflow-visible action lacks a same-ID visible V2 operation. |
| `workflow_operation_action_mismatch` | A visible V2 operation lacks a same-ID workflow-visible action. |
| `task_ingress_feature_required` | A manifest v2+ task provider lacks `task_ingress`. |
| `invalid_notification_provider_delivery_contract` | A notification provider's reserved delivery contract is missing or invalid. |
| `invalid_section_type` | A V2 section is neither an object, list nor reference string. |
| `extension_private_core_import` | Extension runtime code imports private Core instead of public SDK/runtime contracts. |

These compiler/validation issue codes are distinct from the public CLI error
envelope and process exit status. For example, request/service validation errors
can use the outer `validation_failed` code. Record the actual envelope and exit;
do not infer them from a compiler issue or invent an `extension.ui_*` family.

## Install only within the request

When installation is requested and authorized, inspect the archive and run the
existing `extensions install --archive <path>` lifecycle, following its review.
That command works on Development and Scalable installations; on Compact,
install only through the UI's **Install extension from file** or
`POST /api/extensions/install`. An update is the installation of a higher
version; the same or a lower version is refused.
Then use `extensions list`, `extensions show <extension_id>` and
`extensions health <extension_id>` to inspect the installed result. Report what
ran, actual results, archive identity and remaining connection/readiness needs.
Do not install, enable or publish automatically. After an authorized
installation, the extension's operations reach workflow authoring through the
existing knowledge synchronization; confirm them in the installation's UI, or
with its MCP `capability_search` when one is connected. Do not create another
index or execution interface.

---
name: flow-steward-publish-extension
description: Use when a developer wants to publish a Flow Steward extension, or a new version of one, to the public extension catalog Flow-Steward/extensions; covers the repository layout, manifest listing fields, icon, tests, wheels for Linux AMD64 and ARM64, release tags and the catalog pull request.
---

# Publish a Flow Steward Extension

The public catalog is <https://github.com/Flow-Steward/extensions>. Flow
Steward reads its `index.json` and lists the entries under
**Extensions → Catalog**. The catalog holds only a **link** to the author's own
repository; the extension's code and releases live there. The catalog README
(`README.md`, section "Share an extension") is the source of truth: read the
current copy before you start and follow it where it differs from this skill.

Build the extension first with the `flow-steward-extension-authoring` skill.
Publishing does not install anything; never install, enable or publish without
the user's explicit request.

This work needs a terminal with Git and Docker, a Flow Steward application
checkout for the quality gate, and GitHub access (your client's GitHub tools or
an authenticated `gh`) to push tags and open the catalog pull request. It does
not need a Flow Steward MCP connection. When one is missing, say which step it
blocks and do not report that step as done.

## 1. One public repository per extension

- `extension.yaml` sits at the **repository root**.
- Name the repository `ext-<kind>-<implementation>` (for example
  `ext-llm-openrouter`) and give it the GitHub topic `flow-steward-extension`.
- To move an extension out of a larger checkout, the catalog provides
  `scripts/new_extension_repo.py <extension folder> ../ext-<kind>-<name> --repository https://github.com/<owner>/ext-<kind>-<name>`.
  It copies the tracked files and adds the CI and release workflows from the
  catalog's `templates/single-extension/`.
- The id namespace `flowsteward.` is reserved for github.com/Flow-Steward
  (`verified_publishers.json`). Use your own reverse-domain prefix, such as
  `com.acme.crm-sync`.

## 2. Manifest fields the catalog checks

In `extension.yaml`:

- `display_name`: a readable title.
- `description`: at least 40 characters.
- `listing.category`: one id from the catalog's `categories.json` (for example
  `ai`, `crm`, `data`, `ecommerce`, `email`, `messaging`, `other`).
- Optional: `listing.summary` (at most 160 characters; otherwise the first
  sentence of the description), `listing.tags`, `listing.setup_summary`.
- `runtime.contract_version: extension_host_v2`, built on
  `flowsteward-extension-sdk` 0.4.0 or later. Releases without it are not listed.
- `egress` declaring the outbound access (`egress: {}` for none); otherwise
  installation warns `egress_undeclared`.
- `version`: semantic (`1.2.0`). If the bundle has `extension-descriptor.yaml`,
  its `extension_id` and `release_version` must match the manifest.

Next to `extension.yaml`, `icon.png`: PNG only, square, 32–512 px (128×128
recommended), at most 100 KB. A release without a valid icon is refused by the
catalog and by Flow Steward's installer.

Never commit secrets: the check refuses `.env` and key files and any value
under keys such as `password` or `api_key`.

## 3. Validate and test

From a Flow Steward application checkout installed in the Development
environment, run the quality gate against the committed extension checkout:

```bash
./core/entrypoints/cli/scripts/lint.sh --checks extension-static,extension-tests --extension-root /abs/path/to/extension-checkout
```

It stages the checkout under its canonical folder name, validates the manifest,
runs ruff, mypy and bandit, and runs the extension's tests offline. For the
catalog's listing checks, also run `extensions validate` with `--marketplace`
on a copy placed as `extensions/<canonical folder>/` in the application
checkout (do not commit that copy):

```bash
./flow-steward extensions validate <extension_id> --root extensions --health --marketplace
```

`--marketplace` adds the identity, listing, vendor and scope checks. Stop on
any nonzero exit and fix the cause. The CI workflow from the catalog template
(step 5) also runs the catalog's own archive check
(`.github/scripts/catalog_check.py`) on every push.

## 4. Dependencies and architectures

Flow Steward runs on Linux AMD64 and ARM64, and installs offline from the
bundle's `wheels/`.

- **No third-party Python packages**: one archive serves both.
- **Third-party Python packages**: lock the full dependency closure with
  `extensions lock-deps`, then `extensions bundle --with-wheels`. Its default
  platforms are `manylinux2014_x86_64,manylinux2014_aarch64`, so pure-Python
  wheels and compiled wheels for both targets land in `wheels/` of one
  archive.
- **Or one archive per architecture** for compiled wheels (numpy,
  cryptography, onnxruntime...): `<extension_id>-<version>-linux-amd64.zip` and
  `<extension_id>-<version>-linux-arm64.zip`, each with only the wheels for its
  target and a `.fs-package.yaml` naming that target. The catalog's
  `templates/single-extension` packaging script does this when `wheels/` holds
  architecture-specific wheels, and the catalog README describes this layout.
- **Native executable**: one archive per target, each built with
  `flow-steward extensions bundle --runtime-target linux-amd64` (and
  `linux-arm64`), carrying only its own `bin/<target>/`.

A release attaches either one portable archive or per-target archives, never
both. Per-target releases must include `linux-amd64`.

The runtime is CPython 3.12 on glibc 2.36. For packages that publish only
`manylinux_2_28` wheels, pass
`--platforms manylinux_2_28_x86_64,manylinux_2_28_aarch64` to both `lock-deps`
and `bundle`. `extensions validate` does not check both architectures: list
`wheels/` and confirm, for every requirement, an `_x86_64` and an `_aarch64`
wheel or one `any` wheel. If a wheel is missing for one target, stop and report
it; never ship an archive that downloads packages at runtime or silently drops
a target.

## 5. Release

Archive rules the catalog enforces:

- tag `v<version>`, the same version as `extension.yaml`;
- asset `<extension_id>-<version>.zip` (or the per-target names above);
- every file under one top folder named after the id with `.` and `-` replaced
  by `_` (`acme.crm-sync` → `acme_crm_sync/`);
- no symbolic links, at most 50 MB zipped and 150 MB unpacked.

The easiest path is the catalog's template workflows: copy
`templates/single-extension/.github/` (CI on every push: tests, packaging and
the catalog's own archive check; release on every tag), or the simpler
`templates/release-extension.yml`. Then, with the user's go-ahead:

```bash
git tag v1.2.0
git push origin v1.2.0
```

Check that the GitHub Release exists with the expected asset(s).

## 6. First listing: one pull request

Fork `Flow-Steward/extensions` and add exactly one file,
`extensions/<extension_id>.yaml`:

```yaml
repository: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>
```

Open the pull request **from the repository owner's account** (or as a public
member of the owning organization). Do not edit `index.json` or `releases/`;
they are generated. The **Validate submission** check downloads the latest
release and lists what to fix. After the merge the release is listed within
minutes.

## 7. New versions

Bump `version` in `extension.yaml` (and `release_version` in the descriptor),
commit, then push a new `v<version>` tag. **No catalog pull request is needed**:
the catalog checks listed repositories every five minutes and publishes each new
release that passes. A failing release is reported in the catalog's Actions log
and the previous version stays listed.

Never move or replace a published tag or asset. The catalog records each
release's URL, size and SHA-256 once in `releases/<extension_id>/<version>.json`;
if the asset's bytes change later, that release is withdrawn. To fix a release,
publish a new version.

## Report

Return the repository URL, the tag, the release asset name(s) and SHA-256, the
validation and gate results with their exit codes, the catalog pull request URL
(first listing only) and anything not verified, such as installation on ARM64.

---
name: flow-steward-report-issue
description: Use when a Flow Steward user wants to report a bug, a crash, a wrong result or a confusing behavior, or to request a feature, on GitHub Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app; collects the System Diagnostics report and the facts maintainers need.
---

# Report a Flow Steward Bug or Request a Feature

Issues and feature requests go to
<https://github.com/Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app/issues>. Help the user write
one report that a maintainer can act on without a follow-up question. Work with
the user: you collect and draft, the user confirms what is sent.

This skill reports a problem; it does not fix it. Do not change Flow Steward
code, settings or data while preparing a report. A workaround the user can
apply in their own workflow is worth noting in the issue.

What this needs, and what to do without it:

- **GitHub**: your client's GitHub tools or an authenticated `gh` CLI, and the
  user's permission to post on their behalf. Without them, produce the finished
  draft and the link from step 6; the user submits it in the browser. Never
  claim that an issue was filed when it was not.
- **The diagnostics report** comes from the user or their administrator
  (step 2). You do not need a terminal or server access for it.

**Security vulnerabilities are never public issues.** If the problem lets
someone read, change or run something they should not, stop and tell the user
to email `security@flow-steward.org` with the subject prefix `[SECURITY]`, as
`SECURITY.md` in the repository says. Do not file it on GitHub.

## 1. Search first

Search existing issues, open and closed, with two or three key words from the
error message or the feature:

```bash
gh issue list --repo Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app --state all --search "<words>"
```

Without `gh`, open
`https://github.com/Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app/issues?q=<words>`. If an
issue already describes the problem, offer to add a comment with the new facts
(version, diagnostics, steps) instead of opening a duplicate.

## 2. Get the System Diagnostics report

Every bug report needs the diagnostics JSON. It says how the installation is
built and how it runs: the Flow Steward version and image identity, Compact or
Scalable, CPU architecture and resources, database and broker versions, each
service and its health, the installed extensions with their version and state,
and which settings are customised. It has **no logs, no job content and no
setting values** beyond a short list of deployment-shape settings (such as the
profile, storage backend and log level); every configured secret value is
removed wherever it appears.

Ask the user to get it one of two ways:

- **In the UI** (administrator only): **System → Monitoring**, then
  **Download diagnostics**. The file is
  `flow-steward-diagnostics-<UTC stamp>.json`. This is the usual way.
- **From the command line**, by someone with access to the server, in the
  installation folder:

  ```bash
  ./flow-steward reports diagnostics
  ```

  It also collects host facts and the `doctor` result, writes
  `.flow-steward/diagnostics/flow-steward-diagnostics-<UTC stamp>.json` and
  prints the path.

Administrators can also fetch it from the API with
`GET /api/system/diagnostics/report`; an agent does that only when the user
already gave it that access for this purpose. The command-line report is the most
complete, because only the host sees Docker and the containers; prefer it when
the user has access to the server. A non-administrator cannot download the
report; ask the user to get it from their administrator. If the stack is down so badly that neither works, say so in the
issue and include the output of `./flow-steward status` and
`./flow-steward doctor` instead.

Even though the report is redacted, **tell the user to open the file and glance
through it before attaching it**: host names, extension ids and customised
setting names may still be things they prefer not to publish. Never edit the
report to hide a problem; leave out a whole section only if the user insists,
and say in the issue that it was trimmed.

## 3. Collect the facts

- **Version**: from the diagnostics file, or `./flow-steward release info`.
- **What happened**: the exact error text, copied, not paraphrased.
- **Steps to reproduce**: numbered, starting from a known state (which page,
  which workflow or extension, what input). Ask the user to repeat them once
  to confirm the problem still happens.
- **Expected and actual result**: one sentence each.
- **Job**: the job id, the workflow id and the failing step name when a run
  failed. Do not paste the job's data.
- **Screenshots**: of the error or the wrong screen, after cropping out
  customer data, tokens and email addresses.
- **Since when**: did it work before (which version), and what changed (an
  update, a new extension, a setting).

A job page also has **Download full report**. Secrets are redacted in it, but
it contains the job's messages, logs, events and step data, which is often
customer data. Do not attach it to a public issue. Mention that it exists and
offer it privately if a maintainer asks.

## 4. Never publish

Passwords, API keys, tokens, cookies, `.env` contents, connection strings,
private keys, setup links, customer names, emails, orders or file contents.
Check everything you paste — log excerpts and screenshots included. Replace a
value with `<redacted>` when the shape matters.

## 5. Draft the issue

Title: what is wrong, where, in plain words, for example
"Workflow import fails when a child workflow uses a Wait step".

```markdown
## What happened
<exact error text and where it appears>

## Steps to reproduce
1. ...

## Expected
...

## Actual
...

## Environment
- Flow Steward version: <x.y.z>
- Profile: Compact | Scalable
- Job id / workflow id: <if any>
- System Diagnostics report: attached (`flow-steward-diagnostics-<stamp>.json`)

## Notes
<since when, what changed, workaround if any>
```

For a feature request, replace the middle sections with: the problem the user
has today, what they would like to do instead, and how they work around it
now. Diagnostics are optional for a feature request.

Show the draft to the user and get an explicit yes before sending it.

## 6. File it

With an authenticated `gh` (`gh auth status`):

```bash
gh issue create --repo Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app --title "<title>" --body-file issue.md
```

`gh issue create` cannot attach files. After creating the issue, give the user
its URL and ask them to drag the diagnostics JSON (and screenshots) into a
comment in the browser. GitHub accepts `.json` attachments; if their browser
refuses, they can zip the file first.

Without `gh`, open
`https://github.com/Flow-Steward/flow-steward-app/issues/new/choose` and pick
**Bug report** (or **Feature request**). The bug form has a required System
Diagnostics field: the user drags the JSON there. Copy each section of the
draft into its field, attach screenshots, and let the user do the final click.

Report the issue URL back. Do not open more than one issue for one problem.
